analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals and small businesses take statutory claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote, backed by 11 Senate Democrats and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unenforceable for a company to require a person or small business to arbitrate claims that a federal or state statute or constitution was violated. Instead of being routed into private arbitration, those claims could go to court, either one-on-one or as a representative case. Courts, not arbitrators, would decide whether an arbitration agreement applies, and an arbitration award issued in violation of the rule could be thrown out.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals — consumers, workers, and others — and small businesses who would otherwise be forced into private arbitration when a company breaks a federal or state law or a constitution. They could take those claims to a public court, sue in a representative capacity, and have a judge decide whether the arbitration clause applies at all. People whose claims arise after enactment would be covered, and any arbitration agreement signed after a dispute exists would still be honored.

how_it_helps.text: Individuals and small businesses could no longer be forced into private arbitration for claims that a federal or state statute or constitution was violated; those claims could be heard in court, individually or in a representative capacity.

The bill codifies the reasons: it finds that Supreme Court decisions like AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion (2011) and American Express v. Italian Colors (2013) let businesses use arbitration clauses to nullify legal duties Congress created, leaving millions of people unable to vindicate their rights in court.
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the arbitration agreement applies, and an arbitration award resulting from a proceeding that violated the new rule could be vacated.

Companies could still use arbitration for ordinary contract disputes, and an agreement to arbitrate could still be signed voluntarily after a dispute has already arisen — so the bill targets clauses signed before anyone knows there is a problem.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that write mandatory arbitration clauses into consumer, employment, and small-business contracts — banks, credit card issuers, telecom and cable companies, employers, and other businesses — would lose their ability to keep statutory claims out of court. They would face public court proceedings, including representative cases, with the costs and publicity that come with them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with arbitration clauses in contracts

drawbacks.text: Businesses would face more litigation in public courts for statutory claims, and some disputes that arbitration resolves quickly and cheaply — a benefit companies point to — would instead go through slower, more expensive court proceedings.

The bill is narrower than a full arbitration ban: non-statutory contract disputes, and agreements signed after a dispute arises, would remain arbitrable, so many private disputes would still bypass the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring access to public courts for millions of people bound by arbitration clauses — is large, and the bill is deliberately limited: it leaves ordinary contract arbitration alone and even allows arbitration chosen after a dispute exists. The cost falls on companies, which would litigate more claims in open court and lose the confidentiality and speed of arbitration; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices. On balance the bill shifts power over statutory rights from private arbitral forums back to courts, which is its stated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, joined by six original Senate cosponsors.
Ten Democrats in total cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it for the rest of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that put mandatory arbitration clauses in their contracts are better off: they kept the ability to route statutory claims into private arbitration for the rest of the Congress and beyond.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that rely on forced arbitration

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: 10 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Blumenthal, Durbin, Whitehouse, Markey, Hirono, and Coons

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and he never brought it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None supported the bill as sponsor or cosponsor, and the Republican-run committee and chamber never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters were Senate Democrats — the sponsor plus 10 Democratic cosponsors — with no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer lenders
industries.note: These companies are among the heaviest users of mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer contracts. The bill would let consumers take statutory claims — for example under consumer protection laws — to court instead, ending a mechanism that keeps disputes private and out of class actions.

industries.industry: Large employers using mandatory workplace arbitration
industries.note: Millions of workers sign arbitration clauses as a condition of employment. The bill would let them bring statutory claims, such as discrimination and wage claims, in court rather than before a private arbitrator.

industries.industry: Telecom, cable, and other consumer service companies
industries.note: Consumer service contracts commonly require arbitration of statutory claims. The bill would expose these companies to court suits and representative cases from customers and small-business clients.
Arbitrators and arbitration firms earn fees from the disputes the bill would move back into the courts. Removing statutory claims from forced arbitration shrinks their market.
